subject: chemistry
title: Diffusion
welcome_lead: Spray perfume in the corner and minutes later the whole room smells it. Why?
meta_desc: Understand diffusion in gases and liquids in this KS3 chemistry adventure.
final_note: You can now explain diffusion using particles.

concepts.def: Particles spreading from where they are crowded to where they are not.
Gas and liquid particles move in random directions.
How many particles are in a given space.
Particles diffuse from high to low concentration.
Diffusion of scent particles through the air.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Diffusion is the spreading out of particles. It happens because particles in gases and liquids are always moving in random directions.

Spread from crowded to empty.
You smell cookies baking across the kitchen — the smell particles diffuse through the air. A drop of ink in still water slowly spreads out through the liquid.

Diffusion is faster in gases than liquids because gas particles move faster and have more empty space.

It's also faster when the temperature is higher — particles have more energy.

options: Particles spreading out from high to low concentration
Particles freezing in place
A solid melting
Particles disappearing

mcqs.q: What does a mole of a substance represent?
options: Avogadro's number (6.02 x 10^23) of particles of that substance.
SN2 reactions are zero order because they happen in one step.
A mole is a unit of volume equal to 24 dm^3 at any temperature.
A mole is a unit of mass equal to the relative molecular mass in grams of any substance.

mcqs.q: How does the rate of an SN2 reaction depend on concentrations?
options: A mole is a unit of volume equal to 24 dm^3 at any temperature.
Rate is first order in both substrate AND nucleophile (overall second order) because both are involved in the rate-determining step.
SN2 reactions are zero order because they happen in one step.
SN2 reactions are first order overall because only the substrate matters.

mcqs.q: Does a catalyst affect the position of equilibrium?
options: A catalyst increases the yield by being consumed in the forward reaction only.
SN2 reactions are zero order because they happen in one step.
A catalyst shifts the equilibrium towards the products.
No — it speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but at the same position.
